title: Governed by alchemists
author: Christodoulou, Daisy
summary: This piece opens with the Taiping Rebellion — set in motion partly by a Chinese civil-service exam system that guaranteed a large population of frustrated, highly educated but unemployable young men — to introduce a history of the 'formal discipline' theory used to justify Britain's own 1854 Northcote-Trevelyan civil service exam reform, which prioritized classical languages on the belief that studying Greek and Latin trains general reasoning ability transferable to any domain. The author juxtaposes two contemporary justifications for this classical curriculum: Stafford Northcote's sincere claim that translating Thucydides built his reasoning power, against Thomas Macaulay's much stranger argument that the specific content studied is irrelevant — Cherokee or alchemy would work just as well as Greek — because competitive study itself, regardless of what's being competed over, sorts out the ablest people. The piece's central rebuttal to Macaulay is that content does matter: whichever body of knowledge a society's elite are selected on and steeped in shapes what kind of society results, since elites who master a body of knowledge become invested in defending its importance regardless of whether it's true or useful, discouraging any later reassessment of whether the wrong thing was ever being selected for.
points: A specific historical case (the Taiping Rebellion) is used to show how China's civil-service exam system, despite testing genuinely rigorous classical scholarship, produced a large population of frustrated, unemployable, highly educated men — a contributing condition for one of history's bloodiest civil wars.

Britain's 1854 Northcote-Trevelyan civil service reform is shown to have been built on 'formal discipline' theory: the belief that studying Greek and Latin trains a general, transferable reasoning capacity, endorsed personally by reformer Stafford Northcote.

Thomas Macaulay's much stranger, explicitly acknowledged counter-argument is quoted directly: content is irrelevant to the exam's social function, since Cherokee or alchemy would sort the ablest people just as effectively as Greek.

The essay's rebuttal to Macaulay is that content clearly does matter, because whichever knowledge a society selects its elite on shapes what that elite actually knows and can do once in power — 'high-stakes exams don't just identify elites; they determine what the elite knows.'

The piece draws an explicit parallel to today's 'transferable skills' and 'critical thinking' rhetoric, framing modern claims that studying any hard subject builds general problem-solving ability as a direct descendant of Northcote's 19th-century argument.
quotes: In the 200 years before Hong's birth, China's population had doubled, but the number of civil service jobs had stayed the same.

I attribute my own success, such as it has been, entirely to the power of close reasoning which a course of Thucydides, Aristotle…&c., engenders or developes [sic], and to the facility of composition which arises from classical studies.

If, instead of learning Greek, we learned the Cherokee, the man who understood the Cherokee best, who made the most correct and melodious Cherokee verses... would generally be a superior man to him who was destitute of these accomplishments.

He is quite literally arguing that it's acceptable to get teens and young adults to spend years of their lives studying things which are completely false or practically useless, as long as those things are prestigious and fashionable.
As I've written before, in a different context: high-stakes exams don't just identify elites; they determine what the elite knows.
Societies where youths are encouraged to study the arts of war are different to ones where youths are encouraged to study the arts of rhetoric... Stuff matters!
